extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy (readers of Hobbes)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Hobbes's normative principles about the origins and manipulation of religion, the natural condition of mankind, and the first laws of nature (contracts, rights, liberty). Useful for analysing Hobbesian social-contract arguments and criteria for legitimate religious/political authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion of Ghosts (natural seed of religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men naturally conceive of and fear invisible, incorporeal powers (ghosts, spirits, daemons) and therefore form beliefs about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes lists widespread attributions of divinity to elements, animals, places, and abstract qualities (e.g., Chaos, Heaven, Rivers, Muses, Fortune). This natural tendency is a foundational seed from which organized religion grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of second causes (source of religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: People who do not understand causal chains attribute effects to immediate invisible agents rather than to intervening causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because most cannot perceive causal connections, they generalize from observed antecedents and expect similar outcomes; this leads to superstition and the invention of ministerial gods (e.g., Venus for fertility, Apollo for arts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Devotion modelled on human reverence
rubrics_metrics.description: Human worship of invisible powers naturally adopts the same outward expressions used toward other humans: gifts, petitions, thanks, submission, premeditated words, and swearing (invocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reason suggests no further form of worship, these human-like ceremonies become the default, and more elaborate rituals are added by those presumed wiser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking casual things for prognosticks (divination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans are inclined to read the future from casual or coincidental events, turning them into omens or prognostications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes enumerates many divinatory practices (oracles, astrology, augury, entrails, dreams, omens, lottery methods). This tendency fuels superstitious religion and reinforces leaders who exploit it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as cultivated for civil obedience (humane politiques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some religions are invented or shaped by political founders to make people more apt to obedience, lawfulness, peace, charity, and civil society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes religions formed for political ends (used by founders and lawgivers of gentile commonwealths) from those founded by genuine divine revelation (divine politiques). The former function as part of statecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founders' pretended divine origin to legitimize laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and founders of religions often claim their laws and ceremonies derive from gods or divine dictates to ensure acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Numa claiming Egeria's instruction, founders claiming heavenly descent, Muhammad's alleged conferences with the Holy Ghost. Presenting laws as divine reduces suspicion that they are mere human inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aligning civil and divine prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: To enhance obedience, founders make it believed that what the civil law forbids is also displeasing to the gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alignment makes religious transgression tantamount to political disobedience, thus helping rulers maintain order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescribing ceremonies/sacrifices to explain misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Instituting rituals, supplications, and festivals that are said to appease gods explains and controls misfortune, thereby reducing unrest and mutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that when misfortune is attributed to neglected ceremonies, people are less likely to rebel against governors and easier to pacify with pomp and bread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images, temples, and consecrated property to influence the ignorant
rubrics_metrics.description: Material representations and endowed religious institutions are used to impress and control the less educated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptures, consecrated groves, temples, revenues, and dedicated lands make the populace fear and respect the gods (or their human proxies) more readily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instituting ambiguous oracles and divination as social control
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders create or exploit ambiguous prophecies, oracular speech, and various divinatory practices to appear connected to the divine and maintain influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oracles framed ambiguously (or produced under intoxicating conditions) and diverse forms of divination (Delphi, Sibylline books, astrology, necromancy) create an aura of supernatural authority that leaders can exploit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoyning belief of impossibilities (enjoined contradictions undermines wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring belief in logical contradictions is taken as evidence of ignorance in the author of a religion and undermines his credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes asserts that revelation cannot command belief in contradictions; doing so signals lack of wisdom and discredits other claimed revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandalous conduct of religious leaders (undermines sincerity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If founders or ministers behave unjustly, cruelly, profanely, avariciously, or luxuriously, it shows they do not sincerely believe the tenets they preach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct is a stumbling block that makes people doubt the religion; examples include corrupt or immoral priests leading to decline of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private ends/self-interest of religious leaders (undermines love)
rubrics_metrics.description: When leaders benefit personally (dominion, riches, dignity) from religious prescriptions, observers infer self-interest rather than genuine love, discrediting the religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appearance that doctrines promote leaders' private gain makes people suspect manipulative motives and weakens belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony of miracles and prophecy as validating divine calling
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles or true prophecy (extraordinary supernaturals) are the proper testimony to demonstrate divine revelation and a founder's calling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent such supernatural signs, new religious claims obtain only the credence of custom and law of the places where they arose; natural signs are required for inward assent to revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of change in religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion changes when leaders' wisdom, sincerity, or proofs of revelation (miracles) are suspected or fail; scandalous clergy and philosophical contradictions also precipitate revolt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes cites historical examples (Israel's golden calf after Moses's absence; decline of pagan priesthoods due to corruption) to show how faith collapses when leaders fail tests of virtue or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural equality of mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature has made men so equal in body and mind that differences rarely justify claim to exclusive benefits; even the weakest can kill the strongest by cunning or confederacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality in faculties produces equal hope of attaining ends, which is the psychological basis for competition and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal causes of quarrel
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition (for gain), diffidence (for safety), and glory (for reputation) are the three passions that lead men to quarrel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each motive drives violence for different ends: possessions, self-preservation, and reputation (even over trifles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of war (as a continued disposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: War is not only battle but a sustained state in which the will to contend is known over a period of time; where there is no assurance to the contrary there is war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes emphasizes the temporal character of war (like weather) — a few skirmishes don't define war unless the disposition persists; all other time is peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of the state of nature (incommodities of war)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a condition without common power, there is no industry, culture, navigation, arts, knowledge of the earth, letters, society — life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses these consequences to justify establishing common power: insecurity destroys the conditions for civilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions that incline men to peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of death, desire for commodious living, and hope of obtaining these by industry incline men toward peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason suggests articles of peace (laws of nature) by which men may be drawn to agreement; these passions motivate the social contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of Nature (jus naturale)
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty each man has to use his own power as he will for the preservation of his life; the freedom to do whatever, in his judgment, is the aptest means for self-preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This right is the starting point of the state of nature where everyone may use all available means to preserve themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty (absence of external impediments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty properly means absence of external impediments to motion; impediments may reduce power but cannot stop use of remaining power according to judgement and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This physical/practical notion of liberty supports Hobbes's account of rights and obligations in the state of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Nature (lex naturalis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A precept or general rule found by reason forbidding actions destructive of life and prescribing omissions and actions best for preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes RIGHT (liberty to act or forbear) from LAW (which binds to one of those), and uses law of nature as the rational foundation for contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural right to everything in the state of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: In the state of nature every man has a right to everything since he judges any means may help preserve his life against enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This universal right explains the insecurity of life absent common power and motivates laying down rights to achieve peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental law of nature: seek peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental law is that every man ought to endeavour peace as far as he has hope of obtaining it; when he cannot obtain it, he may seek all helps of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first and foundational law of nature; the second branch is the sum of the right of nature (defend oneself by all means).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second law of nature: mutual renunciation of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A man should, when others are willing, lay down his right to all things and be content with so much liberty against others as he would allow them against himself, to achieve peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses the reciprocity underlying contracts (the Golden Rule-like formula) and explains why rights are surrendered for mutual security.

rubrics_metrics.name: What it is to lay down a right
rubrics_metrics.description: To lay down a right is to devest oneself of the liberty of hindering another's use of that same right; it does not confer a new right to another but removes an impediment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes explains renunciation and transfer are voluntary acts signified by words/actions; effects are to create obligations and duties not to obstruct the beneficiary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of renouncing/transferring rights and bonds of obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights are laid aside either by simple renouncing (careless who benefits) or transferring (designated beneficiary). Words, actions, or both are the signs creating bonds; bonds derive strength from fear of consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes notes voluntary acts create obligations, but their enforcement depends on fear of punitive consequences rather than intrinsic force of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all rights are alienable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some rights cannot be understood to be renounced or transferred (e.g., the right to resist someone assaulting you to take your life), because renouncing them would not aim at any good to oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes limits alienability to voluntary acts made for some good to the actor; self-defensive rights are inalienable.
